archetype.name: Pretender (injury-ravaged)
archetype.definition: A 2-2 team whose underlying play ranks near the bottom of the league, now trying to hold its record together with a large share of its starting lineup on the injury report.

report.headline: A .500 record covering for a 31st-ranked team that's losing bodies fast
report.take:
Philadelphia's record says ordinary. The efficiency says this has been one of the worst teams in football. The Eagles are 31st in net EPA, 28th on offense and 24th on defense, and their two wins came by a combined six points over Washington and Tennessee, two offenses ranked 21st and 26th. They were favored by 6 and 7 in those games and failed to cover either. Against the two good defenses they've faced, Chicago and the Rams, they lost by 20 and by 4. They're 0-4 against the spread, which is the market's way of saying it keeps pricing them on reputation and they keep falling short of it.

The offense is the core problem, and it's getting worse. Passing yards have gone 203, 264, 153, 93, and pass EPA swung from +8.8 against Tennessee to -16.5 in Chicago and -8.2 against the Rams. The protection numbers explain much of it. Hurts holds the ball longer than any quarterback in the league (3.2 seconds to throw), and the line gives up a sack on 8.7% of dropbacks, 27th. The run game gets stuffed on 27% of carries, 30th. Overall offensive success rate is 30th. A -5.7% pass rate over expected suggests the staff doesn't trust the dropback game either. This isn't completely new: the 2025 offense already slid to 17th in EPA. But it has fallen off a cliff since then.

The defense is the newer collapse. Last year it ranked 9th in EPA allowed; now it's 24th. There's almost no pass rush (11.2% pressure rate, 31st; hit rate dead last), tackling is poor (14.1% missed, 31st) and the run defense is 29th in EPA allowed. One thing holds up. They rarely get beaten over the top, ranking 6th in deep EPA allowed and 5th and 10th in explosive rush and pass rate allowed. It's a soft-shell unit that gives up a lot of successful plays (25th in success rate allowed) but makes offenses earn them. Special teams at 4 EPA per game, 4th in the league, has quietly covered for a lot.

Then there's the injury report, which may define October. Lane Johnson and backup tackle Fred Johnson are out, and center Cam Jurgens is in the concussion protocol. DeVonta Smith (the target leader with 27 in three games), Dallas Goedert and Hollywood Brown are out. Bigsby is on IR, Barkley is week-to-week, and Baun, Epps, Mitchell and Greenard are out or questionable on defense. This team was already playing at a bottom-five level, and it now heads into Jacksonville missing much of what remained.

strengths.title: Special teams carrying real weight
strengths.body: The Eagles are generating 4 EPA per game on special teams, 4th in the league. For a team scoring 18.8 points a game that's a meaningful share of its margin, and it's part of why two games this bad on offense ended as one-score wins. Special-teams EPA tends to be noisy and regress, so treat it as a real asset that probably won't stay this large.

strengths.title: Defense rarely gets beaten deep
strengths.body: Despite a dead-last pass rush, the defense ranks 6th in deep EPA allowed and 5th in explosive run rate allowed. That points to a conservative, keep-it-in-front structure that forces long drives. It's why points allowed (16th) look far better than EPA allowed (24th). The structure is repeatable, but it depends on the secondary, and Epps is out and Mitchell questionable.

concerns.title: Dropback game is collapsing behind shaky protection
concerns.body: Hurts has the longest time to throw in the league, and the line allows sacks at the 27th-worst rate: 12 in four games, four of them against the Rams. Pass production has fallen in each of the last two games, bottoming out at 93 yards. With Lane Johnson out, Jurgens in the protocol and Smith and Goedert sidelined, both the protection and the targets get worse in the short term. This is a real flaw made acute by injury, not a blip.

concerns.title: No pass rush, poor tackling
concerns.body: A 11.2% pressure rate (31st) and four sacks in four games mean opposing quarterbacks are almost never uncomfortable. Missed tackles at 14.1% (31st) turn short completions into chunk gains. The Rams threw for 317 yards in Week 4. Baun out and Greenard questionable make the second level and the edge thinner still. This looks structural rather than random, so expect it to persist.

concerns.title: Two wins built on thin margins
concerns.body: The wins came by 2 and 4 against bottom-half offenses, with a -0.8 turnover margin per game and a 31st-ranked net EPA underneath. The turnover margin should improve: this franchise was +0.5 and +0.8 per game the last two years. But the efficiency gap is too large for the record to be trusted as is.

trend.note: Pass EPA went from +8.8 in Week 2 to -16.5 and -8.2 in Weeks 3-4, and passing yards have dropped to 153 and then 93. The injury report filled up after the Rams loss, so the next couple of weeks probably get worse before they get better.

nextGame.headline: Banged-up Eagles visit a Jaguars team built to bury them
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville is 3-1, 2nd in net EPA and 2nd in point differential, and its strengths line up with Philadelphia's weaknesses. The Jaguars run the ball efficiently (5th in rush EPA and run success), and the Eagles are 29th against the run. Lawrence gets the ball out quickly (2.75 seconds), which makes a non-existent Eagles rush even less relevant. On defense, Jacksonville smothers the short game (1st in short-pass EPA allowed) and has eight takeaways. That is a bad fit for an offense that holds the ball and has turned it over five times. One opening exists: the Jaguars are 22nd in deep EPA allowed and 24th in explosive pass rate allowed. Their 13.3 points allowed also leans on a 28.6% red-zone TD rate and a +1.5 turnover margin, both likely to cool.

Availability tilts the game further. Philadelphia is without both Johnsons at tackle, likely without Jurgens (concussion protocol), and without Smith, Goedert, Brown and Bigsby. Barkley is questionable. Defensively, Baun and Epps are out, and Mitchell and Greenard are questionable. That leaves Wicks, Lemon and Cooper as the receiving corps and a patched line against the AFC's most opportunistic defense. Jacksonville has secondary issues of its own: CB Montaric Brown and CB Braswell are out, and safeties Murray and Ransaw are questionable. That deep-ball weakness is real if Hurts has time and anyone to throw to.

keyMatchups.title: Jaguars run game vs Eagles front
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville's ground game ranks 5th in EPA and gets 91% of short-yardage conversions. Philadelphia is 29th in rush EPA allowed and will be missing Baun, a 97%-snap linebacker. If the Jaguars stay on schedule, they control the clock and the Eagles' offense gets few possessions.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a thinned secondary
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville is the best team in the league against short passes but 22nd against deep ones. With Montaric Brown out, the secondary is thinner. Jacksonville also ranks 25th in pressure rate, so Hurts' long time to throw may hurt less than usual. The catch is that the Eagles' best receivers are out, so someone among Wicks, Lemon and Cooper has to win downfield.

keyMatchups.title: Turnover battle and the red zone
keyMatchups.body: Jacksonville leads the league at +1.5 turnovers per game and holds opponents to TDs on 28.6% of red-zone trips. Philadelphia is -0.8 per game and turned it over three times in its blowout loss. Both Jaguar numbers are likely to regress over a season, but over one game they're the most likely path to a lopsided score.

nextGame.watch: Whether a patched-up Eagles line, missing Lane Johnson and likely Jurgens, can give Hurts enough time to attack Jacksonville's vulnerable deep secondary before the turnovers come.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule gives Philadelphia room to recover. Two games against Dallas (31st-ranked defense), plus Washington, Arizona, Indianapolis and an 0-4 Houston, is a soft middle stretch. Most of the injury return estimates are short-term, apart from Bigsby. The turnover margin should also drift toward this franchise's recent positive norm. On the other side, special-teams EPA at this level and the one-score wins are the parts most likely to regress. The missing pass rush and the protection problems look structural rather than random, and the offense had been sliding since 2025.

The realistic picture is a team that gets healthier and plays closer to average, not back to the 2024 level. A fully healthy group probably sits in the middle of the league in efficiency. Against this schedule that means hovering around .500 and contending in a weak NFC East, where every rival also has two losses or more. The 2020 season, when a similar profile produced four wins, is the downside if the injuries linger.
swingFactors: Health of the offensive line, especially Lane Johnson and Jurgens
Whether the pass rush finds any pressure
Turnover margin reverting toward the recent positive norm

bets.reason: The net EPA gap is enormous (2nd vs 31st), and the Eagles are 0-4 ATS even when healthy. Their best receiver, tight end, both tackles and possibly their center are now out. Jacksonville's run game and quick passing attack target exactly what this defense does worst.

The spread and total imply about 17.75 points for Philadelphia, close to its 18.8 average. That average came with a healthier lineup, and the offense ranks 30th in success rate. Jacksonville takes the ball away and is stingy in the red zone, so the under is the lean, tempered by Jacksonville's deep-ball leaks and the likely regression of its red-zone numbers.

confidence.note: Only four games of data and an unusually long, fluid injury list. The direction is clear, but the size of the drop is uncertain.
